title: Two British Indian Men Assaulted Outside Dussehra, Bathukamma Celebration in West Yorkshire
excerpt: The attack outside Ossett Town Hall on October 17 left both men bleeding, police are treating the assaults as racially aggravated, and organisers are pressing for CCTV to be secured before it is overwritten.
body:
• Two British Indian Telugu Hindu men were assaulted outside Ossett Town Hall, West Yorkshire, on Saturday night, October 17, during a Dussehra and Bathukamma celebration, in an attack police are treating as racially aggravated, The Times of India reported.
  • The 51-year-old victim told TOI he was pushed to the ground, left bleeding from the face, and punched in the left eye; his friend suffered a head injury and a bleeding hand. No arrests have been made.
  • Event organisers, in a formal statement published by INSIGHT UK, say masked youths questioned attendees through the evening and have asked West Yorkshire Police to secure CCTV before footage is routinely overwritten.
  • Anyone who was near Ossett Town Hall that evening, or who has footage, is being urged to come forward to West Yorkshire Police — organisers say witness material is the fastest route to identifications.

Two British Indian men were assaulted outside a Dussehra and Bathukamma celebration in Ossett, West Yorkshire, on Saturday night in what police believe was a racially aggravated attack, The Times of India reported. The celebration, organised by local Telugu Hindu community groups, was being held at Ossett Town Hall on October 17, with families and children among those inside.

What happened outside the hall

Earlier in the evening, a group of around 25 local youths, mostly male, were riding e-bikes around the hall, asking organisers what was going on inside and who was there, TOI reported. Some tried to force their way in and were turned away by security.

https://x.com/INSIGHTUK2/status/2112149860098904085

One of the victims, a 51-year-old British Indian man originally from the Hyderabad region, left the event at around 9pm and walked to his car with a friend. They encountered a group of eight to 10 youths, some wearing black balaclavas.

"He hit me hard and pushed me to the ground on my face and left me bleeding. I stood up and then he punched me in my left eye. My friend was left with a head injury and his hand was bleeding."

— The 51-year-old victim, speaking to The Times of India

The organisers' own account, published as a formal statement by INSIGHT UK, adds a timeline: masked individuals questioning an organiser outside at about 8:30pm, a volunteer carrying a box approached by three people on electric bikes at about 9pm, and the two attendees attacked at about 9:15pm roughly 10 yards from the hall by a group estimated at 10 people aged 16 to 20. A larger group of 15 to 20 young people then gathered outside, some attempting to enter, before police officers arrived at about 10:30pm to take statements. Community officers later escorted attendees to their cars.

Police response, and what organisers are asking for

There have been no arrests so far. Inspector Andrew Dickinson of West Yorkshire Police said, according to TOI: "We recognise the distress this has caused to the wider Hindu community. We are treating these assaults seriously and are working to ensure those responsible are held accountable."

The organisers' statement asks police to confirm the incidents have been formally recorded with crime reference numbers, take full statements from the two injured men and other witnesses, and secure CCTV covering the hall and surrounding streets — warning that footage may be overwritten under routine retention periods. They have also asked the council and venue management to record the incident and review stewarding and access arrangements for future community events at the hall, and asked police to examine whether the evidence points to a hate-related or discriminatory element.

Why this lands hard in the diaspora

Dussehra and Bathukamma are family festivals: Bathukamma, Telangana's floral festival, is built around women and children arranging flower stacks and singing together. An attack at the door of a town-hall celebration — on men walking to their car after being warned it was not safe to leave with family, per the organisers' account — is the kind of incident that changes how community groups across Britain plan every festival that follows: more stewards, earlier finishes, escorted walks to car parks.

For now, the practical steps are the ones the organisers have named. Anyone who was near Ossett Town Hall on the evening of October 17, or who holds phone, dashcam or doorbell footage from the surrounding streets, is urged to contact West Yorkshire Police. The investigation's next visible milestone will be whether police issue crime reference numbers and an appeal for witnesses — and whether any arrests follow before the festival season's remaining events.
